findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized ORDER BY clause
findings.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL statements to extract, modify, or delete database records, bypassing authorization controls
findings.evidence: Line 24: `const rows = await db.query(\`SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE owner_id = $1 ORDER BY ${order}\`, [req.user.id]);` - The 'order' parameter from req.query is directly interpolated into the SQL string without parameterization or validation. While a default value is provided, user input is trusted entirely. An attacker can supply values like '(CASE WHEN ...) -- ' to execute arbitrary SQL.
findings.recommendation: Use a whitelist of allowed column names. Example: const ALLOWED_COLUMNS = { 'created_at': 'created_at', 'amount': 'amount' }; const column = ALLOWED_COLUMNS[req.query.order] || 'created_at'; then use parameterized query with the column name sanitized.

findings.title: Missing authorization check on /invoices/:id endpoint
findings.impact: An authenticated attacker can access invoices belonging to other users by guessing or enumerating invoice IDs, leading to unauthorized disclosure of financial data
findings.evidence: Line 8-10: `const invoice = await db.query('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]); res.json(invoice);` - No check for req.user.id or owner_id. Compare with /receipts/:id (line 15-16) which correctly includes `AND owner_id = $2` check. The endpoint trusts the id parameter without verifying ownership.
findings.recommendation: Add owner_id check: `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2` with parameters [req.params.id, req.user.id]. Return 404 if no matching invoice found to avoid information leakage.

findings.title: SSRF vulnerability in fetchLogo function
findings.impact: An attacker can make the server fetch arbitrary URLs, including internal services (localhost, private IP ranges), metadata endpoints (AWS/GCP), or trigger attacks on external targets. Can lead to information disclosure, credential theft, or DoS.
findings.evidence: Lines 5-8: `async function fetchLogo(url) { const response = await fetch(url, { redirect: 'follow' }); return Buffer.from(await response.arrayBuffer()); }` - No hostname validation, no URL parsing, accepts arbitrary URLs. The ALLOWED allowlist (line 2) is defined but only used in fetchAsset(), not fetchLogo(). The 'redirect: follow' allows an attacker to chain redirects from public URLs to internal services.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same validation as fetchAsset(): parse the URL, validate hostname against allowlist, use redirect: 'error'. Or accept only data: URIs / base64-encoded images: `if (!url.startsWith('data:')) throw new Error('only data: URLs allowed');`

findings.title: JWT signature verification missing (authentication bypass)
findings.impact: An attacker can forge arbitrary JWT tokens with any user ID or claims, completely bypassing authentication. All access controls depend on req.user.id being trustworthy.
findings.evidence: Lines 4-8: `function currentUser(req) { const bearer = (req.headers.authorization || '').replace('Bearer ', ''); const claims = jwt.decode(bearer); return { id: claims && claims.sub, role: claims && claims.role }; }` - The jwt.decode() function decodes without signature verification. This is different from jwt.verify() which checks the signature. An attacker can create a valid-looking JWT with any payload and the server will trust it.
findings.recommendation: Replace jwt.decode() with jwt.verify(bearer, process.env.JWT_SECRET); Also at line 12 in tagRequest(). Store JWT_SECRET securely in environment variables. Handle errors with try/catch and return 401 if verification fails.

findings.title: Stored XSS vulnerability in invoiceNote function
findings.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript that executes in the browser of other users viewing the same invoice, enabling session hijacking, credential theft, or malware distribution
findings.evidence:
Lines 4-6: `function invoiceNote(note) { return \`
${note}
\`; }` - The note parameter is directly interpolated into HTML without any escaping. Contrast with customerName() (lines 9-11) which correctly uses escapeHtml(name). An attacker can create an invoice with note='' or ''
findings.recommendation:
Use escapeHtml() like customerName() does: `function invoiceNote(note) { return \`
${escapeHtml(note)}
\`; }` Also implement Content-Security-Policy headers to limit XSS blast radius.
